ahmadiyya.1: Converts are embraced by a global family, with an instant role and hospitality.
ahmadiyya.2: Community help arrives through the same structure that records your contributions.
ahmadiyya.3: Members are promised nearness to God and burial in the Wasiyyat cemetery.
ahmadiyya.7: "No compulsion in religion" is taught, yet former members report an expected boycott.
ahmadiyya.9: Aam leads to Wasiyyat, which leads to new schemes, and each sacrifice exposes the next.
ahmadiyya.10: Chanda Aam is called "compulsory", yet voluntary chandas are refused from non-payers.
ahmadiyya.12: A member complaining about an office-bearer becomes the problem for "creating disorder".
ahmadiyya.14: Marriage, friendship and leisure are centered on the jamaat.
ahmadiyya.17: Organized critics are framed as conspiracies against the Jamaat.

catholicism.1: A wounded person is folded into parish life with the promise of finally belonging.
catholicism.2: Catholic parishes, schools and charities often provide real material help.
catholicism.3: Catholicism offers a massive future economy: heaven, purgatory, indulgences and sainthood.
catholicism.4: A lapsed Catholic may be approached with guilt-heavy language like "Come home".
catholicism.5: Catholicism can devalue through inherited guilt, original sin, mortal sin and shame.
catholicism.6: Questioning clerical authority gets "You are rejecting the Church Christ founded".
catholicism.7: A conscience contradicting the Magisterium is taught to be malformed.
catholicism.8: Grace arrives through sacraments the institution meters, and the peace wears off.
catholicism.9: A Catholic receives absolution, but the shame remains and deeper repentance is needed.
catholicism.10: Catholic teaching can sound absolute in doctrine but flexible in pastoral application.
catholicism.11: Catholic hierarchy may accuse critics of attacking the Church.
catholicism.12: Clerical abuse is denied, minimized, transferred, buried in process or reframed.
catholicism.13: Children may be normalized early into confession, mortal sin, guilt and penance.
catholicism.14: Catholic isolation often works through institutional authority and warnings against error.
catholicism.15: You are rarely just disagreeing with a local priest, but with the Church across centuries.
catholicism.16: A lapsed Catholic is pressured by parents, priests and relatives: "Go to confession".
catholicism.17: Critics of clerical abuse may be framed as anti-Catholic, rebellious or secularized.
catholicism.18: Abuse survivors may face diocesan bureaucracy, canonical process and institutional delay.
catholicism.19: Children receive sacraments before they can understand what Catholic identity implies.
catholicism.20: Catholicism can bind people through guilt and relief, from mortal sin to absolution.
catholicism.21: A Catholic tries confession, penance and obedience but still feels unworthy.
catholicism.22: Catholic authority presents restrictions on sexuality and marriage as loving guidance.
catholicism.23: Priests are called Father and the Church Mother, so laypeople remain spiritual children.
catholicism.24: Catholic identity can absorb the person through sacrament, family, school and parish.
catholicism.25: Suffering is bypassed through "offer it up", penance and obedience.
catholicism.26: Catholic financial control can appear through parish giving, tuition and diocesan appeals.
catholicism.27: Catholic crisis language may center secularism, moral collapse and attacks on the family.
catholicism.28: A Catholic who challenges clerical abuse may be treated as lapsed or rebellious.
catholicism.29: A questioning layperson leaves, and parish life continues with another volunteer.
catholicism.30: If conscience agrees with Church authority it is conscience, and if not, malformed.

eastern-orthodoxy.1: The convert is enchanted by incense, icons, chanting, liturgy and ancientness.
eastern-orthodoxy.2: Converts may receive intense hospitality, from meals after liturgy to spiritual direction.
eastern-orthodoxy.3: Orthodoxy offers theosis, becoming united with God, and so a powerful hook.
eastern-orthodoxy.4: Those who leave Orthodoxy may be told they are abandoning the fullness of the faith.
eastern-orthodoxy.5: Eastern Orthodoxy can devalue through relentless emphasis on the passions and pride.
eastern-orthodoxy.6: A convert senses authoritarian control, and the response is "That is your pride".
eastern-orthodoxy.7: Converts are told Orthodoxy is freedom from legalism, then handed fasting rules.
eastern-orthodoxy.8: The fading glow is diagnosed as a slackening prayer rule, so the rule thickens.
eastern-orthodoxy.9: Converts are first told "Come and see", then they must fast, confess and obey a priest.
eastern-orthodoxy.10: Orthodoxy often says it is not legalistic, yet believers may face strict expectations.
eastern-orthodoxy.11: Orthodoxy may accuse converts who leave of pride, while demanding deep submission.
eastern-orthodoxy.12: A parishioner reports clerical control and is told "You are prideful".
eastern-orthodoxy.13: Converts are slowly accustomed to fasting cycles, confession and long liturgies.
eastern-orthodoxy.14: Eastern Orthodoxy can isolate converts by teaching them to distrust Western Christianity.
eastern-orthodoxy.15: Orthodoxy triangulates through spiritual fathers, saints and "the mind of the Church".
eastern-orthodoxy.16: A questioning convert hears concern about pride from priest, godparent and elders.
eastern-orthodoxy.17: A person leaving Orthodoxy may be labeled proud, spiritually deluded or unstable.
eastern-orthodoxy.18: Concerns about priestly control are met with a private talk with the priest.
eastern-orthodoxy.19: Converts "freely" enter Orthodoxy after being told it is the fullness of the faith.
eastern-orthodoxy.20: Orthodoxy calls itself a hospital for the soul while stressing sickness and unworthiness.
eastern-orthodoxy.21: A believer tries questioning and is told that questioning proves delusion.
eastern-orthodoxy.22: The Church is framed as a hospital for the soul, and priests as physicians.
eastern-orthodoxy.23: The spiritual father model can position adult believers as patients or children.
eastern-orthodoxy.24: Converts may gradually replace their previous identity with an Orthodox convert identity.
eastern-orthodoxy.25: Pain is bypassed through humility, repentance, obedience and fasting.
eastern-orthodoxy.26: Orthodox parishes may rely on donations, stewardship pledges and building funds.
eastern-orthodoxy.27: Orthodoxy may frame the modern West as spiritually diseased.
eastern-orthodoxy.28: A convert celebrated as having "come home" may be dismissed as prideful after leaving.
eastern-orthodoxy.30: Orthodoxy can say "We do not have a legalistic rule system" while pressuring fasting.

islam.1: A new convert may be celebrated with hugs, meals, gifts and invitations to iftar.
islam.2: A new Muslim may receive meals, gifts, Qurans, Arabic lessons and social protection.
islam.3: Islam offers paradise as the ultimate deferred reward, with safety from hell.
islam.4: A Muslim who distances from Islam may be told "Come back to salah".
islam.5: Institutional Islam can devalue by emphasizing human weakness and ingratitude.
islam.6: A Muslim questions a rule and is told "You are following your desires".
islam.7: A questioning Muslim is told Islam commands knowledge, but conclusions are pre-approved.
islam.8: The sweetness of iman is felt in Ramadan, and its absence is read as sin.
islam.9: A convert is first celebrated, then expectations escalate and questioning must stop.
islam.10: "No compulsion in religion" may be quoted, while pressures make exit socially dangerous.
islam.11: Islamic authorities may accuse critics of arrogance while demanding obedience to clerics.
islam.12: A person reports abuse and the response may be denial, then accusations of slander.
islam.13: A convert gradually accepts increasing regulation of prayer, food, dress and family life.
islam.14: Islam can isolate through the ummah as primary belonging and warnings against dunya.
islam.15: Islam can triangulate through family, imam, mosque, spouse and fear of outsiders.
islam.16: A Muslim who questions mosque authority may hear "Don't embarrass the family".
islam.17: Apostates or critics may be labeled arrogant, corrupted by the West or immoral.
islam.18: A person reports abuse and is told to be patient and not damage the ummah.
islam.19: A convert says the shahada in a warm community, then discovers the social expectations.
islam.20: The believer is taught fear of hell, then receives relief through prayer and the ummah.
islam.21: A person asks about doubt and is told to increase iman and avoid Shaytan.
islam.22: Families may control clothing, marriage and friendships while saying they protect faith.
islam.24: Muslim identity can reorganize the entire self: name, dress, diet and daily schedule.
islam.25: Abuse or family control may be bypassed with sabr, duʿa or "Allah knows best".
islam.26: Islamic communities may use zakat, mosque donations, school tuition and charity drives.
islam.27: Islamic communities may manufacture crisis through fears of hell, apostasy and fitna.
islam.28: A Muslim who doubts or leaves prayer may be treated as spiritually dangerous.

mormonism.1: Missionaries offer friendship and meals long before the convert understands obligations.
mormonism.2: Missionaries offer free labor and friendship before the investigator understands the cost.
mormonism.3: Mormonism future-fakes with eternal families, exaltation and temple blessings.
mormonism.4: A less-active Mormon may receive sudden friendliness from people who ignored them before.
mormonism.5: Mormonism can devalue through worthiness interviews and sexual purity standards.
mormonism.6: A member raises historical problems, and the answer is "Doubt your doubts".
mormonism.7: Personal revelation is authentic only when it confirms the prophet.
mormonism.8: Worthiness runs on renewable approval: temple recommends expire and are retaken.
mormonism.9: Told to pray about the Book of Mormon, testimony must then become baptism and tithing.
mormonism.10: "I know the Church is true" can mean different things depending on challenge.
mormonism.11: LDS leaders may accuse former members of being offended, lazy learners or deceived.
mormonism.12: A member raises historical concealment, and the Church denies wrongdoing.
mormonism.13: Children and teens may be normalized into worthiness interviews and bishop authority.
mormonism.14: Mormonism can isolate through ward life, church schools and approved media.
mormonism.15: Mormonism triangulates through bishop, prophet, spouse, parents and deceased ancestors.
mormonism.16: A doubting member may receive visits from ministering brothers, missionaries and bishops.
mormonism.17: Former members may be described as offended, lazy learners, bitter or prideful.
mormonism.18: A member asks about history and receives correlated answers or invitations to pray harder.
mormonism.19: Children say they "choose" baptism at eight in a world where it is expected.
mormonism.20: LDS life bonds through family eternity, worthiness, testimony and community belonging.
mormonism.21: Members ask about history and are told to pray, doubt doubts and trust leaders.
mormonism.22: Bishops, worthiness interviews and tithing are framed as loving covenant care.
mormonism.23: Adults meet with bishops for worthiness approval, sexual confession and tithing status.
mormonism.24: LDS identity can absorb the whole self: testimony, garments, tithing and callings.
mormonism.25: Historical problems are bypassed with "continuing revelation" or "focus on the basics".
mormonism.26: LDS financial control is direct through tithing, missionary costs and fast offerings.
mormonism.27: LDS manufactured crisis may center eternal families and staying on the covenant path.
mormonism.28: Former members may lose callings, temple access, ward belonging and family trust.
mormonism.30: The Church says members have agency, while temple access depends on obedience.

pentecostal-charismatic.1: First-visit prayer by name, a ride home, a meal and an immediate invitation to serve.
pentecostal-charismatic.2: Flood relief, school fees paid, funerals covered and rent bridged are genuine.
pentecostal-charismatic.3: A specific prophetic word: this year is your year, the business will open.
pentecostal-charismatic.4: Members who drift are called back with a new word or a special service.
pentecostal-charismatic.5: Poverty, illness and childlessness are diagnosed as spiritual conditions.
pentecostal-charismatic.6: A member says the harvest did not come and is told they misheard the word.
pentecostal-charismatic.7: Give beyond your means and you are commended for faith.
pentecostal-charismatic.9: The seed was too small, then the timing was wrong, then the harvest was spiritual.
pentecostal-charismatic.10: "Sow a significant seed", and significant is never defined, so members compete upward.
pentecostal-charismatic.11: Members who ask about finances are described as having a spirit of greed.
pentecostal-charismatic.12: The ministry becomes the persecuted party and the members become the aggrieved defenders.
pentecostal-charismatic.13: Closing the doors during the offering and calling givers forward by amount.
pentecostal-charismatic.14: Friends outside are "not going where you're going".
pentecostal-charismatic.17: Departing members are named from the pulpit as offended, backslidden or under attack.
pentecostal-charismatic.18: Direct questions about accounts are met with silence, deflection or a change of topic.
pentecostal-charismatic.20: The ministry that diagnoses your spiritual condition is the ministry that relieves it.
pentecostal-charismatic.22: Prophetic direction over marriage, business and medical decisions is framed as care.
pentecostal-charismatic.24: Members are renamed, reassigned and rebuilt around ministry roles.
pentecostal-charismatic.25: Grief, depression and abuse are answered with deliverance rather than medicine or therapy.
pentecostal-charismatic.26: Seed faith, first fruits, prophetic offerings and perpetual building funds.
pentecostal-charismatic.27: Recurring emergencies with deadlines: the property will be lost, the window closes Sunday.
pentecostal-charismatic.30: No membership roll, no minutes, no constitution and no published accounts.

seventh-day-adventism.1: Bible studies in your home, meals brought, and a Sabbath community that holds a full day.
seventh-day-adventism.3: Prophetic certainty about a Sunday law, imminent for a century and a half.
seventh-day-adventism.4: Lapsed members are visited, revisited and invited to revival weeks.
seventh-day-adventism.5: Your record is under review in a heavenly court, and the outcome is not disclosed.
seventh-day-adventism.6: A member cites the church's own study and is told they misunderstand inspiration.
seventh-day-adventism.10: "Lesser light" is authoritative but subordinate, a status never operationally defined.
seventh-day-adventism.17: Walter Rea lost his church employment in 1980, after his findings were reported.
seventh-day-adventism.18: Questions about the investigative judgment are answered with "it is settled".
seventh-day-adventism.19: "The church has spoken" follows votes many members did not know were happening.
seventh-day-adventism.30: "Lesser light" functions as a decisive status, and the gap is the deniability.

soka-gakkai.12: The 1970 apology denied any intent to obstruct speech.

unification-church.1: Recruiters approach strangers in a friendly way while hiding the church's name.
unification-church.2: Community care comes first, and obligation follows.
unification-church.3: The promise is lineage salvation and freed ancestors.
unification-church.4: Families pull members back, especially in the second generation.
unification-church.5: The teaching names a fallen lineage and Japan's national guilt.
unification-church.6: Court findings are described as persecution.
unification-church.7: Free will is set against ancestral obligation.
unification-church.8: Sacrifice is praised, and doubt meets silence.
unification-church.9: A source describes daily pressure to donate, with karma attached to money.
unification-church.10: Legal analysis describes "donations" as solicited through sales of goods.
unification-church.11: Critics are cast as greedy lawyers.
unification-church.12: Victims and courts are recast as persecutors.
unification-church.13: Recurring offerings are treated as ordinary devotion.
unification-church.14: Workshops, communal life and matched marriage isolate members.
unification-church.15: Parents, leaders and the True Parents align on marriage and giving.
unification-church.16: Relatives press second-generation members to marry within the lineage.
unification-church.17: Critics and lawyers are portrayed as anti-religious activists.
unification-church.18: Recovery has run through lawsuits by the lawyers' network.
unification-church.19: Marriages are matched through the Blessing, and a "choice" is made inside it.
unification-church.20: Shared persecution narrative binds members to leaders.
unification-church.21: Families are unable to recover savings without lawyers.
unification-church.23: Adults' marriages are chosen for them.
unification-church.24: Selfhood is defined as lineage position.
unification-church.25: Loss is reframed as indemnity paid.
unification-church.26: Donations and spiritual sales are the means of financial control.
unification-church.27: Urgent campaigns are tied to ancestors' suffering.
unification-church.28: Those who leave are cut off from lineage and family.
unification-church.29: The second generation fills the pews.
